upham: Upham, N.S., Esselstyn, J.A. & Jetz, W. (2019). Inferring the mammal tree: species-level sets of phylogenies for questions in ecology, evolution, and conservation. PLoS Biology 17: e3000494. Node-dated MCC tree of the completed 5,911-species posterior (topology-constrained, birth-death); node heights and 95% HPDs
alvarez: Álvarez-Carretero, S., Tamuri, A.U., Battini, M. et al. (2022). A species-level timeline of mammal evolution integrating phylogenomic data. Nature 602: 263-267. 4,705-species timetree (mean ages, 95% CIs)
common_source: IUCN Red List 2026-1 (GBIF checklist doi:10.15468/0qnb58), preferred English name

overrides.name: Panthera
overrides.cite: Figueiró, H.V. et al. (2017). Genome-wide signatures of complex introgression and adaptive evolution in the big cats. Science Advances 3: e1700299, Fig. 1A. doi:10.1126/sciadv.1700299
overrides.reason: Upham's tree puts the snow leopard with the lion and leopard and the tiger outside the rest (2.34, 1.90 and 4.91 Ma); the genome-wide species tree (64% of windows) has tiger + snow leopard vs jaguar + (lion, leopard). Node ages and 95% HPDs are read from Fig. 1A's labels (the figure is 313 px wide, so the last digit is +-0.02; research/panthera-split-dates.md).

overrides.name: Felis catus
overrides.cite: Driscoll, C.A. et al. (2007). The Near Eastern origin of cat domestication. Science 317: 519-523. doi:10.1126/science.1139518
overrides.reason: The domestic cat is the wildcat's tamed form (from the Near Eastern wildcat), so it parts from the wildcat at domestication, not at Upham's 0.94 Ma speciation; the earliest tamed cat was buried with a person on Cyprus ~9,500 years ago (Vigne et al. 2004, Science 304: 259).

overrides.name: Sahelanthropus tchadensis
overrides.cite: Brunet, M. et al. (2002). A new hominid from the Upper Miocene of Chad, Central Africa. Nature 418: 145-151. doi:10.1038/nature00879
overrides.reason: Possibly the earliest hominin, possibly a stem hominine; this tree's Homo-Pan split (6.15 Ma) is younger than its 7.2 Ma first appearance, so it branches off the stem of both.

overrides.name: Orrorin tugenensis
overrides.cite: Wood, B. & Boyle, E.K. (2016). Hominin taxic diversity: fact or fantasy? American Journal of Physical Anthropology 159 (S61): 37-78. doi:10.1002/ajpa.22902
overrides.reason: An early hominin (bipedal femora); it branches off the human lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Ardipithecus kadabba
overrides.cite: Wood, B. & Boyle, E.K. (2016). American Journal of Physical Anthropology 159 (S61): 37-78. doi:10.1002/ajpa.22902
overrides.reason: An early hominin; it branches off the human lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Australopithecus ramidus
overrides.cite: White, T.D. et al. (2009). Ardipithecus ramidus and the paleobiology of early hominids. Science 326: 64-86. doi:10.1126/science.1175802
overrides.reason: Open Tree keeps its original genus (Australopithecus ramidus, White et al. 1994); White et al. 1995 moved it to Ardipithecus, the name it is known by, given here as its label. It branches off the human lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Australopithecus anamensis
overrides.cite: Wood, B. & Boyle, E.K. (2016). American Journal of Physical Anthropology 159 (S61): 37-78. doi:10.1002/ajpa.22902
overrides.reason: The earliest australopith; it branches off the human lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Australopithecus afarensis
overrides.cite: Kimbel, W.H. & Delezene, L.K. (2009). Yearbook of Physical Anthropology 52: 2-48. doi:10.1002/ajpa.21183
overrides.reason: Lucy's species, often taken as the ancestor of later hominins (from A. anamensis by anagenesis); it branches off the human lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Kenyanthropus platyops
overrides.reason: A contemporary of A. afarensis, of debated affinity; it branches off the human lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Australopithecus deyiremeda
overrides.cite: Haile-Selassie, Y. et al. (2015). Nature 521: 483-488. doi:10.1038/nature14448
overrides.reason: A contemporary of A. afarensis; it branches off the human lineage within its range (3.5-3.3 Ma), at 3.45 Ma so that it does not tie with K. platyops's 3.5 Ma.

overrides.name: Australopithecus africanus
overrides.cite: Wood, B. & Boyle, E.K. (2016). American Journal of Physical Anthropology 159 (S61): 37-78. doi:10.1002/ajpa.22902
overrides.reason: The Taung child's species; it branches off the human lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Paranthropus aethiopicus
overrides.cite: Wood, B. & Boyle, E.K. (2016). American Journal of Physical Anthropology 159 (S61): 37-78. doi:10.1002/ajpa.22902
overrides.reason: The earliest robust australopith (the Black Skull); the Paranthropus lineage leaves the human lineage here.

overrides.name: Australopithecus garhi
overrides.reason: Found with early stone-tool cut marks at Bouri; it branches off the human lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Panthera zdanskyi
overrides.cite: Mazák, J.H., Christiansen, P. & Kitchener, A.C. (2011). Oldest known pantherine skull and evolution of the tiger. PLoS ONE 6: e25483. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0025483
overrides.reason: The most primitive member of the tiger lineage (2.55-2.16 Ma); it branches off at its first appearance. Several later studies treat it as a synonym of P. palaeosinensis.

overrides.name: Homo habilis
overrides.cite: Spoor, F. et al. (2007). Nature 448: 688-691. doi:10.1038/nature05986
overrides.reason: Early Homo; it branches off the human lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Paranthropus boisei
overrides.cite: Wood, B. & Constantino, P. (2007). Yearbook of Physical Anthropology 50: 106-132. doi:10.1002/ajpa.20732
overrides.reason: East Africa's later robust australopith, widely taken as P. aethiopicus's descendant.

overrides.name: Homo rudolfensis
overrides.cite: Wood, B. & Boyle, E.K. (2016). American Journal of Physical Anthropology 159 (S61): 37-78. doi:10.1002/ajpa.22902
overrides.reason: Early Homo beside H. habilis; it branches off the human lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Panthera gombaszoegensis
overrides.cite: Chatar, N., Michaud, M. & Fischer, V. (2022). Not a jaguar after all? Phylogenetic affinities and morphology of the Pleistocene felid Panthera gombaszoegensis. Papers in Palaeontology 8: e1464. doi:10.1002/spp2.1464
overrides.reason: Treated as the jaguar's ancestor ("P. onca gombaszoegensis", Hemmer 1971); first appearance ~1.9-2.0 Ma (O'Regan 2002; records from ~1.5 Ma to a doubtful >2.7 Ma). Contested: the first phylogenetic analysis places it closer to the tiger. The dataset's first appearance (3.96 Ma) sits on the old crown date and is not used.

overrides.name: Homo erectus
overrides.reason: The first long-legged, Africa-leaving Homo; it branches off the human lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Paranthropus robustus
overrides.cite: Herries, A.I.R. et al. (2020). Science 368: eaaw7293. doi:10.1126/science.aaw7293
overrides.reason: South Africa's robust australopith; it branches off the Paranthropus lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Australopithecus sediba
overrides.cite: Berger, L.R. et al. (2010). Australopithecus sediba: a new species of Homo-like australopith from South Africa. Science 328: 195-204. doi:10.1126/science.1184944
overrides.reason: Described as a descendant of A. africanus; it branches off that lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Homo georgicus
overrides.cite: Lordkipanidze, D. et al. (2013). A complete skull from Dmanisi, Georgia, and the evolutionary biology of early Homo. Science 342: 326-331. doi:10.1126/science.1238484
overrides.reason: The Dmanisi hominins, usually counted as early H. erectus; it branches off that lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Homo antecessor
overrides.cite: Welker, F. et al. (2020). The dental proteome of Homo antecessor. Nature 580: 235-238. doi:10.1038/s41586-020-2153-8
overrides.reason: Its enamel proteome puts it as a close sister of the lineage of Neanderthals, Denisovans and modern humans; it branches off the human lineage at its first appearance.

overrides.name: Homo naledi
overrides.cite: Berger, L.R. et al. (2017). Homo naledi and Pleistocene hominin evolution in subequatorial Africa. eLife 6: e24234. doi:10.7554/eLife.24234
overrides.reason: Small-brained but late (335-236 ka); its place in Homo is unresolved. It branches off the human lineage at 0.9 Ma, a placeholder inside Homo's crown, not a dated split.

overrides.name: Homo floresiensis
overrides.cite: van den Bergh, G.D. et al. (2016). Homo floresiensis-like fossils from the early Middle Pleistocene of Flores. Nature 534: 245-248. doi:10.1038/nature17999
overrides.reason: The Flores 'hobbit'. Its likely ancestors are the Mata Menge hominins (~0.7 Ma), usually derived from H. erectus (a more primitive source is argued too); it branches off H. erectus there.

overrides.name: Homo neanderthalensis
overrides.cite: Prüfer, K. et al. (2014). The complete genome sequence of a Neanderthal from the Altai Mountains. Nature 505: 43-49. doi:10.1038/nature12886
overrides.reason: Their high-coverage genome puts the split of Neanderthal and modern human populations at 550-765 ka (Prüfer et al. 2014); their band starts at Sima de los Huesos, ~430 ka.

overrides.name: Panthera spelaea
overrides.cite: de Manuel, M. et al. (2020). The evolutionary history of extinct and living lions. PNAS 117: 10927-10934, SI Table S3. doi:10.1073/pnas.1919423117
overrides.reason: The cave lion's nuclear genome dates its split from the lion at 470 ka (392-529 ka; X-chromosome PSMC 495 ka, 460-578 ka). The mitogenomes give 1.89 Ma (Barnett et al. 2016).

overrides.name: Panthera balamoides
overrides.cite: Stinnesbeck, S.R. et al. (2020). Panthera balamoides and other Pleistocene felids from the submerged caves of Yucatán. Historical Biology 32: 930-939. doi:10.1080/08912963.2018.1556649
overrides.reason: Described from Yucatán caves and compared with the jaguar; it branches off the jaguar's lineage at its first appearance. Contested: Blaine et al. 2019 and Ruiz-Ramoni et al. 2019 argue it is a short-faced bear (Arctotherium).

overrides.name: Canis familiaris
overrides.cite: Perri, A.R. et al. (2021). Dog domestication and the dual dispersal of people and dogs into the Americas. PNAS 118: e2010083118. doi:10.1073/pnas.2010083118; Freedman, A.H. et al. (2014). Genome sequencing highlights the dynamic early history of dogs. PLoS Genet 10: e1004016. doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1004016; Skoglund, P. et al. (2015). Ancient wolf genome reveals an early divergence of domestic dog ancestors and admixture into high-latitude breeds. Curr Biol 25: 1515-1519. doi:10.1016/j.cub.2015.04.019
overrides.reason: The dog lineage split from the grey wolves', and dogs were domesticated, in Siberia by ~23 ka (Perri et al. 2021, archaeology and genetics together). The genomes date the split from 14.9 ka (13.9-15.9 ka; Freedman et al. 2014, at mu = 1e-8 and 3-year generations) to 27-40 ka (Skoglund et al. 2015, calibrated on the 35 ka Taimyr wolf): the interval here. 23 ka sits inside it and is older than the domestic stock's start (anchors.DOMESTICATION_YEAR, ~15 ka).

common.1488: Nabarlek (English, from Australian Kunwinjku Aboriginal language)
